message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"5e15c4f71bf38f53adbe6049c8795f59defa8dc900a700507bbc128db4016247","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-fl-class-e:lineage:59","source_registry_sha256":"b17b1a3691c9724cc739459037987900e5b1edce40443ad13e42b6eee3e12974","units":[{"unit_id":"sec06-u01","module_id":"sec06-m01","objective_ids":["sec06-u01"],"title":{"text":"Pavement lines and lane markings","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Pavement lines tell you where you may drive, change lanes and pass, often before any sign does.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Jo is behind a slow truck on a two-lane road with a solid yellow line on Jo's side and a broken line on the other side.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A solid-right pair bars passing for the driver on the solid side, while a broken-right pair permits it.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]},"result":{"text":"Jo must not pass until the line on Jo's side becomes broken.","fact_ids":["sec06-R03"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a center turn lane can be used to pass slow traffic.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04"]},"correction":{"text":"Center lanes serve left turns from both directions but are never used for passing.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F04"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Broken on your side, you may pass; solid, you may not.","fact_ids":["sec06-R03"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You see a double white line between two lanes going your way. May you cross it to change lanes?","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02"]},"answer":{"text":"No, double white lines are never crossed.","fact_ids":["sec06-R02"]},"rationale":{"text":"White broken lines allow changes, solid lines are avoided, and doubles are never crossed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Reading the pavement","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03","sec06-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Edge and lane lines","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03","sec06-F04"]},{"text":"Yellow line pairs","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03","sec06-F04"]},{"text":"Lane arrows and special lanes","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03","sec06-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"The paint on the road is a set of instructions, and this lesson teaches you to read it. Lines along the edges frame the road, white on the right and yellow on the left on a divided road. Lines between lanes tell you whether traffic beside you moves the same way or the opposite way, and whether you may change lanes or pass. Then come stop lines, lane arrows, center turn lanes, reversible and bicycle lanes, and finally curb paint and striped areas that tell you where not to park or drive at all. Every one of these markings carries a rule, so we will take them in order from the edges inward.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03","sec06-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":45,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"White and yellow lane lines","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"White divides same-way traffic","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},{"text":"Broken white: change lanes; solid: avoid; double: never cross","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},{"text":"Yellow divides opposing traffic; broken yellow: pass from the right","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"White lines divide lanes of traffic moving the same way. A broken white line means you may change lanes, a solid white line means you should avoid crossing it, and a double white line is never crossed. Yellow lines divide traffic moving in opposite directions. A broken yellow line can be crossed to pass from the right side when it is safe. So color tells you which way the neighboring traffic moves, and the pattern of the line, broken, solid or double, tells you what you may do about it. Color first, pattern second: that is how to read any lane line you meet on the road.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Yellow line pairs","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Double solid: no crossing except left turns and bike passes","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]},{"text":"Solid on your side: no passing","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]},{"text":"Broken on your side: passing allowed","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Yellow lines often come in pairs. Two solid yellow lines bar all crossing, except to turn left or to pass a bicycle. When one line is solid and one is broken, look at the line on your side. A solid line on your right side, nearest you, bars your passing. A broken line on your side permits passing when it is safe. In a worked example, Jo is behind a slow truck with a solid yellow line on Jo's side. Jo must not pass until the line on Jo's side becomes broken, even if the road ahead looks clear. When the two lines differ, the one nearest you is the one that decides what you may do.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":47,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Stop lines, arrows and center lanes","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop at the stop line, before the crosswalk","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"ONLY arrows force the turn; mixed arrows free it","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"Center lanes: left turns both ways, never passing","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"A stop line fixes the point where you stop, before any crosswalk, and walkers in the crosswalk always have the right of way. A lane marked with an arrow and the word ONLY forces the turn shown. A lane with mixed arrows lets you choose among the directions shown. A center lane serves left turns for traffic in both directions, but it is never used for passing. So the lane markings decide both where you stop and which way you are allowed or required to go from each lane you choose. Stop lines and arrows are painted instructions, and they bind you just as a sign does.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Special lanes and curbs","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Reversible lanes flip with rush hours","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-R05"]},{"text":"Exclusive bike lanes walled off by solid white; sharrows share","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-R05"]},{"text":"Yellow curbs: no parking; fire lanes and safety zones: no entry","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Reversible lanes change direction with rush hours and are controlled by signals. Exclusive bike lanes are separated by a solid white line, and cars cross them only to turn when the lane is empty. Sharrow markings mean bicycles and cars share the lane. A yellow curb means no parking. Diagonal stripes guard obstacles, and fire lanes and safety zones may not be entered at all. These markings protect particular users of the road, from cyclists to emergency crews, so respect each one exactly as painted. Each special lane has its own users, so check the paint before you enter or cross it.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Center lanes are not for passing","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-R02","sec06-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Center lane: left turns from both directions","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-R02","sec06-R03"]},{"text":"Never use it to pass","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-R02","sec06-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"The trap is treating the center turn lane as an extra lane for passing slow traffic. The handbook says center lanes serve left turns from both directions but are never used for passing. A related trap is the double white line. It looks like an ordinary lane line, but a double white line is never crossed. And with yellow pairs, always read the line on your side: solid means no passing, broken means passing is allowed when safe. Each of these markings has one meaning, so read it before you move. Read each marking for what it says, not for what would be convenient at the moment.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-R02","sec06-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the double white rule","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"A double white line between lanes","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02"]},{"text":"May you cross it to change lanes?","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: a double white line separates two lanes going your direction. May you cross it to change lanes? Settle on your answer before going on. The answer is no. White lines divide same-direction traffic: broken white lines allow lane changes, solid white lines are avoided, and double white lines are never crossed. So even when the lane next to you is empty, a double white line between you and it means you stay where you are. Broken white is the only white line that invites a lane change, so a double white line keeps you in your lane every time.","fact_ids":["sec06-R02","sec06-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Pavement markings recap","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03","sec06-F04","sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-R01","sec06-R02","sec06-R03","sec06-R04","sec06-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Color shows direction, pattern shows permission","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03","sec06-F04","sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-R01","sec06-R02","sec06-R03","sec06-R04","sec06-R05"]},{"text":"Read the line on your side","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03","sec06-F04","sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-R01","sec06-R02","sec06-R03","sec06-R04","sec06-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"To recap, keep your lane except to turn, exit or shift, with white edge lines on the right and yellow on the left. White divides same-way traffic, with broken lines changeable, solid avoided and doubles never crossed, while yellow divides opposing traffic. Double solid yellows bar crossing except left turns and bike passes, and the line on your side decides passing. Stop at stop lines, follow ONLY arrows, use center lanes only for left turns, and respect bike lanes, sharrows, yellow curbs and fire lanes. Paint is a rule, not a suggestion.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03","sec06-F04","sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-R01","sec06-R02","sec06-R03","sec06-R04","sec06-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec06-u02","module_id":"sec06-m02","objective_ids":["sec06-u02"],"title":{"text":"Sign colors and regulatory signs","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Sign colors tell you what kind of message is coming, and regulatory signs set rules you must obey.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F09"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Two cars arrive at an all-way stop at the same moment, side by side.","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-R08"]},"reasoning":{"text":"All-way stops clear in arrival order, and right-side ties go to the right.","fact_ids":["sec06-F09"]},"result":{"text":"The car on the right goes first.","fact_ids":["sec06-F09"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a yield sign always requires a full stop.","fact_ids":["sec06-R08"]},"correction":{"text":"A yield sign means slow for crossing traffic; it does not require a halt unless needed.","fact_ids":["sec06-R08","sec06-F10"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Stop halts, yield slows.","fact_ids":["sec06-R08"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Two cars reach an all-way stop together, one on the other's right. Which goes first?","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-R08"]},"answer":{"text":"The car on the right.","fact_ids":["sec06-F09"]},"rationale":{"text":"All-way stops clear in arrival order, with right-side ties broken rightward.","fact_ids":["sec06-F09"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Colors and rule signs","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"What sign colors mean","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]},{"text":"Guide sign numbering","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]},{"text":"Stop, yield and rule plates","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Signs speak a color code, and this lesson teaches it first. Each color names a family of signs, from red for stop and yield to brown for recreation. Then we look at guide signs and how their route numbers work, along with the blue and brown signs that point to services and scenic places. Finally we cover regulatory signs: stop and all-way stops, yield, entry bans and wrong-way signs, speed plates, lane-use and turn plates, and plates that control passing, reserved lanes and stopping on the shoulder. Learn the colors first, because they help you read every other sign faster.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The color code","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red: stop and yield; orange: work; yellow: warning","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-R06"]},{"text":"Fluorescent: school and walkers; black and white: rules","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-R06"]},{"text":"Green: guidance; blue: services and disabled bays; brown: recreation","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Sign colors follow a code. Red is for stop and yield signs. Orange marks work zones. Yellow is for general warnings, and fluorescent colors mark school zones and pedestrian crossings. Black and white signs state rules. Green signs give guidance, blue signs point to services and mark disabled parking, and brown signs point to recreation. Each color names one sign family, so the color alone tells you what kind of message to expect, often before you can read the words on the sign itself. When you see a color from a distance, you already know what family of message is coming.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Guide signs","fact_ids":["sec06-F08","sec06-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Even numbers run east and west","fact_ids":["sec06-F08","sec06-R07"]},{"text":"Odd numbers run north and south","fact_ids":["sec06-F08","sec06-R07"]},{"text":"Exits match mile markers; blue for services, brown for scenic sites","fact_ids":["sec06-F08","sec06-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Green guide signs carry route numbers with a pattern. Routes with even numbers run east and west, and routes with odd numbers run north and south. Exit numbers match the mile markers. Blue and white signs point to services such as food and fuel, and brown and white signs point to scenic and historic sites. So green guides your route and distance, blue tells you where to find services, and brown tells you where the scenery and history are. The pattern helps you navigate without a map. Even east-west, odd north-south, and exits that match the mile markers.","fact_ids":["sec06-F08","sec06-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Stop, yield and no entry","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-F10","sec06-R08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop: full halt at the line, crosswalk or sight point","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-F10","sec06-R08"]},{"text":"All-way stop: arrival order; ties go right","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-F10","sec06-R08"]},{"text":"Yield: slow, halt only if needed; wrong way: reverse at once","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-F10","sec06-R08"]}],"narration":{"text":"A stop sign demands a full stop at the stop line, the crosswalk or the point where you can see. At an all-way stop, cars go in the order they arrived, and when two arrive together the car on the right goes first. In a worked example, two cars arrive side by side at the same moment, so the car on the right goes first. A yield sign means slow for crossing traffic, without a required stop unless needed. Entry bans and wrong-way signs mean you must reverse the mistake at once, and a red slash forbids whatever it pictures. Each of these signs asks for a different action, so name the action before you move.","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-F10","sec06-R08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":46,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Speed, lane and turn plates","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-R09","sec06-R10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Speed, exit-speed and doubled-fine zone plates","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-R09","sec06-R10"]},{"text":"Lane-use plates assign turns and shared centers","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-R09","sec06-R10"]},{"text":"Turn bans: U, side, red-light, all; one-way and keep-right","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-R09","sec06-R10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Speed plates cap the speed on a road, exit-speed plates cap it on a ramp, and zone plates double fines when their lights are on. Lane-use plates assign left turns, shared center lanes, mandatory turns and right entries that must yield to bicycles going straight. Turn bans cover U-turns, side turns, turns on red, all turns and forced turns, while one-way, keep-right and slower-traffic-keep-right plates channel the flow. Each ban names the move it forbids, so read the plate before you start the turn. The plates are short, but each one carries a specific rule for that stretch of road.","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-R09","sec06-R10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Yield is not a full stop","fact_ids":["sec06-R08","sec06-F10","sec06-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yield: slow for crossing traffic","fact_ids":["sec06-R08","sec06-F10","sec06-F09"]},{"text":"Stop only if needed","fact_ids":["sec06-R08","sec06-F10","sec06-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"The trap is treating a yield sign like a stop sign. A stop sign always demands a full halt. A yield sign asks you to slow for crossing traffic and give way, stopping only if you need to. The opposite mistake happens at all-way stops, where some drivers rush. The rule there is arrival order, with ties going to the car on the right. Keep the three signs apart: stop means halt fully, yield means slow and give way, and an entry ban or wrong-way sign means reverse your mistake at once. Stop means halt, yield means give way, and an entry ban means turn back.","fact_ids":["sec06-R08","sec06-F10","sec06-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the all-way stop","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-R08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two cars arrive together","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-R08"]},{"text":"Which one goes first?","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-R08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: two cars reach an all-way stop at the same moment, and one is on the right of the other. Which car goes first? Settle on your answer before going on. The answer is the car on the right. All-way stops clear in the order cars arrive, and when two arrive together the tie goes to the car on the right. Every car at an all-way stop still makes a full stop at the line, the crosswalk or the point where the driver can see cross traffic. Arrival order decides first, and the right-side rule only breaks a tie between cars that arrive together.","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-R08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Signs recap","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-F09","sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-F13","sec06-R06","sec06-R07","sec06-R08","sec06-R09","sec06-R10","sec06-R11"]},"lines":[{"text":"One color, one family","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-F09","sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-F13","sec06-R06","sec06-R07","sec06-R08","sec06-R09","sec06-R10","sec06-R11"]},{"text":"Stop halts, yield slows","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-F09","sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-F13","sec06-R06","sec06-R07","sec06-R08","sec06-R09","sec06-R10","sec06-R11"]}],"narration":{"text":"To recap, red is for stop and yield, orange for work, yellow for warning, fluorescent for school and walkers, black and white for rules, green for guidance, blue for services and disabled bays, and brown for recreation. Even routes run east and west, odd routes north and south. Stop signs demand full halts, all-way stops clear in arrival order with ties to the right, yields slow without a required halt, and plates control speed, lanes, turns, passing, reserved lanes and shoulders. Read the color, then the words. Each color names its family.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-F09","sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-F13","sec06-R06","sec06-R07","sec06-R08","sec06-R09","sec06-R10","sec06-R11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec06-u03","module_id":"sec06-m03","objective_ids":["sec06-u03"],"title":{"text":"Warning passing.","fact_ids":["sec06-R13"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"What do curve warning plates order drivers to do?","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R13"]},"answer":{"text":"Slow down and do not warn you","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-F15","sec06-F16","sec06-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"Advance warnings","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-F15","sec06-F16","sec06-F17"]},{"text":"Road changes and conditions","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-F15","sec06-F16","sec06-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"Warning signs are mostly yellow diamonds, and their job is to give you time. This lesson groups them. Some warn ahead of signals, stops, yields and lower speed limits, often with an advisory plate showing a safe speed. Others announce changes in the road, such as merges, lane drops, roundabouts and the start or end of a divided highway. Curve and crossroad plates tell you to slow and scan. Crossing plates flag places where others may enter the road, and condition plates flag low spans, loose surfaces and narrow bridges. Each group gives you time to slow down before you reach the place it warns about.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-F15","sec06-F16","sec06-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Advance warnings","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-R12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yellow diamonds warn ahead of signals, stops and yields","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-R12"]},{"text":"Also ahead of lower speed limits","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-R12"]},{"text":"Advisory plates post curve-safe speeds","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-R12"]}],"narration":{"text":"Yellow diamond signs warn of signals, stop signs, yield signs and lower speed limits ahead. They do not replace those controls; they let you prepare for them. An advisory plate under a warning posts a speed that is safe for a curve. In a worked example, Alex sees a curve warning with an advisory speed plate. Alex slows to the advisory speed before the curve and does not pass while in it. The advance warning plus the advisory plate together tell Alex what is coming and how fast to take it safely. The warning comes first, so you have time to adjust before the control itself.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-R12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Curves and crossroads","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Bends, sharp hooks, S-curves, winding roads","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R13"]},{"text":"All order slower speeds and no passing","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R13"]},{"text":"Crossroads: scan left and right","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Curve plates come in several shapes: a simple bend, a sharp hook, an S-curve and a winding road.
